report.verdict: A flat headline hides a sharp mix shift: August 2026 US commercial GGR slipped 0.6% YoY to $6.48bn as sports betting revenue fell 15.6% to $1.00bn on a 160bp hold collapse (9.2% vs 10.8%) and handle that is now shrinking in every month without a World Cup, while iGaming (+12.3% to $1.03bn) out-earned sportsbooks for the month and retail casino held steady (+0.9%). For an operator, the regulated US sportsbook is now a share-and-tax fight against an untaxed, federally-sheltered prediction-market competitor whose legal status is heading to the Supreme Court; iGaming remains the growth vertical but is locked in seven states with no new launches in 2026.
summary: **Headline: first YoY decline of 2026.** AGA's Commercial Gaming Revenue Tracker (released 21 Oct 2026, compiled from state regulator reports across 38 commercial jurisdictions) puts August 2026 commercial GGR at $6.48bn, -0.6% YoY, versus +8.6% in July (World Cup) and a record $7.06bn in May. Oklahoma had not reported July/August, so a small upward revision is possible.

**Sports betting is the entire drag.** Sportsbook GGR fell 15.6% to $1.00bn on handle of $10.89bn (-0.7%); national hold dropped to 9.2% from 10.8%. Roughly 160bp of hold compression explains ~$175m of the ~$185m YoY revenue shortfall — this is a margin print, not yet a demand collapse, but handle is the structural worry.

**Handle has shrunk in every non-World-Cup month since December 2025.** AGA states explicitly that outside June–July (World Cup; July handle +31.9% to $11.60bn) handle has been down YoY since Dec-25, blaming (i) sports event contracts on CFTC-registered prediction markets and (ii) a later college-football start. State data corroborate: New York mobile handle -15.2% to $1.73bn (flattered base from a single Fanatics whale in Aug-25), New Jersey sports revenue -25.0% to $61.4m, Pennsylvania -19.9% to $39.4m, Michigan AGR -29.3%.

**iGaming now out-earns sports betting in a month.** Online casino GGR rose 12.3% to $1.03bn (YTD $8.11bn, +17.4%) across only seven states (NJ, PA, MI, CT, WV, DE, RI). Growth is decelerating (+15.7% July, +27.6% CY2025) with 'no new markets coming online'; Maine is the only pending launch (AGA expected late 2026; delay risk flagged by trade press).

**Retail casino is stable, not growing.** Traditional slot and table GGR +0.9% to $4.44bn (slots $3.25bn +1.0%; tables $885.9m +2.1%, helped by Resorts World NYC's expansion). Nevada statewide win +3.1% to $1.27bn with the Strip flat (+0.7% to $684.1m) and Las Vegas visitation -4.3% to 3.0m; Pennsylvania retail tables -18.1%; New Jersey total gaming revenue -4.1%.

**Online penetration: ~31% of August GGR, 34.5% in CY2025.** iGaming plus sports betting (96.5% of which was online in 2025) totalled $2.03bn in August; AGA's CY2025 tracker put online at 34.5% of the $78.72bn total (30% in 2024). In 12 states the majority of commercial revenue is now online; in NJ, PA and MI iGaming exceeds brick-and-mortar.

**Tax take fell with sportsbook margins.** Regulated gaming generated $1.46bn of state gaming tax in August (-1.5%); sports betting tax -14.0%. Implied blended take ~22.5% of GGR. CY2025 direct gaming taxes were $17.86bn (+12.3%) per State of the States 2026 — note AGA's Feb-2026 tracker cited $18.09bn (+15.1%); the gap is a definitional/revision difference we could not reconcile.

**Tax regime: state GGR-based, wide dispersion, ratcheting up.** Online sports betting GGR tax runs from 6.75% (NV, IA) to 51% (NY); Illinois layers a $0.25/$0.50 per-wager surcharge on a 20–40% graduated rate; New Jersey lifted both online casino and online sports to 19.75% (from 15%/13%) from 1 Jul 2025; Louisiana 21.5% online (from 15%); Maryland 20% online (from 15%). Ohio and Michigan rejected hikes. Federal excise of 0.25% of handle plus $50 per sportsbook employee applies on top. Pennsylvania's iGaming effective tax was ~45.6% in FY2025/26 ($1.34bn on $2.93bn).

**Player-level federal tax hit from 2026.** The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed 4 Jul 2025) caps deductible gambling losses at 90% of losses from tax year 2026, creating phantom taxable income for break-even bettors; the FAIR BET Act to restore 100% has stalled in the House. This disproportionately affects high-volume sharp/VIP customers and is an incremental headwind to regulated handle.

**Prediction markets are the structural competitor — untaxed and un-licensed at state level.** Kalshi's August notional volume was $37.17bn (-7.3% MoM); Kalshi + Polymarket (incl. Polymarket US) $45.33bn (-14.5% MoM, first fall in a year, after a $50.59bn July record); sports were ~83% of Kalshi's July volume. Volume is not handle-equivalent (notional, two-sided, high-frequency), but the order of magnitude vs $10.89bn regulated handle is the point. AGA estimates >$1.56bn of state gaming tax foregone since Jan-2025 (up from ~$0.5bn cited in Feb-2026).

**Legal status is now a circuit split headed to SCOTUS.** Third Circuit (6 Apr 2026, 2–1, KalshiEX v. Flaherty) held sports event contracts are likely 'swaps' under the CEA with CFTC exclusive jurisdiction pre-empting New Jersey gambling law (preliminary-injunction stage). Ninth Circuit (28 Aug 2026, 3–0) ruled the opposite for Nevada, refusing to enjoin the Nevada GCB. Cert petitions were filed 2–11 Sep 2026 (New Jersey, Robinhood, reportedly Crypto.com); none granted as of this report. CFTC event-contract rulemaking (comments closed 30 Apr 2026) remains pending.

**Congress is moving toward state primacy.** Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz plans to file, after the 3 Nov midterms, a bill barring prediction markets from listing gambling-linked (incl. sports) event contracts without state or tribal authorisation (Bloomberg Law, 16 Oct 2026). If enacted it would re-fence the regulated sportsbook market — the single largest swing factor for 2027 handle.

**Operator landscape: a duopoly under pressure at the top.** In New York (the largest market, 8 mobile licensees, 51% tax) DraftKings led handle for a second month ($614.0m, 9.2% hold, $56.3m GGR) ahead of FanDuel ($599.6m, 10.7% hold, state-high $64.0m GGR), then Fanatics ($213.2m), BetMGM (~$120m), Caesars ($112.4m), with BetRivers, theScore Bet and Bally Bet trailing. Nationwide share data were not disclosed in the release [unverified].

**Licensing is state-by-state and tethered to land-based assets.** Post-PASPA (Murphy v. NCAA, 2018) each state legislates its own regime; most online skins are tied to casino/racetrack/tribal licences or capped mobile licences (e.g., New York's 9-licence model), with suitability vetting, in-state servers/geolocation and multi-million-dollar fees and renewals. 493 commercial casino locations operate in 27 states; 38 jurisdictions have commercial casinos and/or sports betting; tribal gaming (IGRA) sits outside these AGA totals.

**Untaxed grey verticals are the AGA's enforcement agenda.** The release names three channels that pay no state gaming tax — skill machines, 'sweepstakes casinos' and prediction-market sports contracts. Several states enacted sweepstakes prohibitions in 2025–26 [state list not re-verified this cycle]; enforcement intensity is rising and is a tailwind for licensed iGaming in the states that have it.

**Payments and RG rules are state-set; no federal online framework.** UIGEA (2006) governs payment processing for unlawful online gambling; licensed operators rely on ACH/online banking, debit, PayPal/Venmo-type wallets and prepaid cards, with several states barring credit-card funding and mandating deposit/time limits, self-exclusion and 21+ KYC [specific state rules not re-verified this cycle]. No numeric payments or RG statistics are disclosed in the AGA release (n/a).

**Read-through for B2Tech.** The US is a 38-jurisdiction patchwork with the highest absolute online revenue pool in the world but (a) a tax ratchet, (b) a CAC-heavy duopoly, (c) a federally-sheltered untaxed competitor and (d) stalled iGaming expansion. The asymmetric opportunity is B2B/platform supply into iGaming states and into any post-SCOTUS/Cruz re-fencing of sports betting, rather than a B2C sportsbook entry at today's economics.

segments.name: Sports betting (online + retail)
segments.headline: Revenue -15.6% on a 160bp hold miss and structurally soft handle; prediction markets and a late college-football start cited by the AGA; NY, NJ, PA and MI regulator data all confirm the slide.
narrative: National sportsbook GGR of $1.00bn in August 2026 compares with an implied $1.185bn a year earlier. Handle slipped only 0.7% to $10.89bn, so almost the entire revenue decline is hold: 9.2% versus 10.8%. The AGA is explicit that, outside June and July (World Cup; July handle +31.9% to $11.60bn and GGR +27.0% to $1.27bn), handle has declined year-on-year every month since December 2025. That makes August the first 'clean' post-tournament month and a better guide to the underlying trend than the summer prints: month-on-month, GGR fell 21.3% and handle 6.1%. Year-to-date GGR is still up 4.0% at $10.45bn, but that cushion was built in Q1 (favourable hold) and the World Cup.

The AGA attributes the softness to two factors: sports event contracts on CFTC-registered prediction markets, which it regards as 'illegal sports betting' that pays no state gaming tax, and a later start to the college-football calendar (fewer Week-0/Week-1 fixtures in August). The second factor is one-off and will reverse in the September print; the first is structural and, on the volume evidence, large. Kalshi's total notional volume was $37.17bn in August (about 82% of the sector), with sports around 83% of its July volume, so even allowing for two-sided counting and market-maker churn the product is clearly absorbing a meaningful slice of US event-betting demand without a state licence, state tax or state RG obligations.

State regulator data are consistent with a national margin squeeze rather than a collapse in activity. New York (NYSGC) reported mobile handle of $1.73bn (-15.2% YoY, but the Aug-25 base was inflated by a single Fanatics customer) and GGR of $168.5m (-5.4%) at a 9.7% hold; DraftKings led handle for the second consecutive month ($614.0m, 9.2% hold, $56.3m GGR) while FanDuel took the most revenue ($599.6m handle, 10.7% hold, $64.0m GGR; hold down from 11.9%). Fanatics ($213.2m), BetMGM (~$120m, 10.5%) and Caesars ($112.4m, 9.1%) followed; BetRivers, theScore Bet and Bally Bet are sub-scale. New Jersey (DGE) sports wagering gross revenue fell 25.0% to $61.4m (online $59.7m, -24.6%; YTD $671.4m, -5.3%), which the DGE attributed to the later fall calendar and a lower win percentage. Pennsylvania (PGCB) sports wagering revenue fell 19.9% to $39.4m. Michigan adjusted gross receipts fell 29.3% on handle -2.5%.

The regulatory cost base keeps rising. Online GGR tax ranges from 6.75% (Nevada, Iowa) to 51% (New York); Illinois applies a 20–40% graduated rate plus a $0.25/$0.50 per-wager surcharge (a repeal bill, HB 5143, was filed in February 2026); New Jersey moved to 19.75% from 13% (1 Jul 2025); Louisiana 21.5% online/10% retail; Maryland 20% online/15% retail; Ohio stayed at 20% after a 40% proposal failed. The 0.25% federal excise on handle and $50 per-employee head tax sit on top. With national hold at 9.2%, a 51% New York operator retains roughly 4.5c per $1 wagered before promotions, payments, data and marketing — only the two scale leaders can run that model profitably.

Commercially, August says three things to a prospective entrant. First, the regulated handle pool is no longer growing organically; growth in 2025 (+11.0% to $166.94bn) came from new states (Missouri launched December 2025 and only one new state launched in the year to July 2026) and tournaments. Second, hold is normalising after the 2025 parlay-driven record (10.16% for the year), so revenue forecasts built on 10%+ holds are at risk. Third, the competitive perimeter is undefined until the Supreme Court or Congress rules on event contracts. A B2C entry today buys into a duopoly, a tax ratchet and an untaxed competitor; the better-risked exposure is B2B pricing/risk, trading or platform supply, and optionality on a re-fenced market if the Cruz bill or a Ninth-Circuit-style SCOTUS outcome prevails.

segments.name: iGaming (online casino)
segments.headline: +12.3% to $1.03bn — now a larger monthly pool than sports betting, but decelerating with seven states and no 2026 launches; NJ slowed to +4.4%, PA to ~+6%.
narrative: Online casino GGR of $1.03bn in August 2026 (+12.3% YoY, +2.0% MoM) took iGaming above sportsbook revenue for the month. Year-to-date GGR is $8.11bn (+17.4%), following $10.74bn (+27.6%) in CY2025, when December became the first $1bn+ month. The AGA's framing is 'natural maturation': growth has stepped down from +27.6% (2025) to +15.7% (July) to +12.3% (August) because the state footprint has not changed since Rhode Island (2024). Michigan, New Jersey and Pennsylvania account for roughly 90% of the national total, and in those three states iGaming now exceeds brick-and-mortar casino revenue.

State prints show the deceleration is broad. New Jersey internet gaming win rose 4.4% to $259.3m — described locally as the lowest return since February and, for a second month, below Atlantic City's land-based win — though YTD it is still +13.2% at $2.13bn. Pennsylvania's August iGaming (slots $195.2m +8.8%, tables $48.1m -2.6%, poker $2.4m -5.2%) summed to about $245.7m, roughly +6% YoY, after $249.0m (+9.1%) in July; its FY2025/26 iGaming revenue was $2.93bn (+18.4%) carrying $1.34bn of tax (~45.6% effective). Michigan's iGaming grew 32% in 2025 and remains the strongest of the big three, but August state data were not captured here [n/a].

Tax and licensing economics differ materially from sports betting. iGaming is taxed on GGR at rates from New Jersey's 19.75% (raised from 15% on 1 Jul 2025) to Pennsylvania's split rate (slots far higher than tables; ~46% blended) and effective rates above 50% in some racino-style states; licences are tethered to land-based casinos or tribal compacts, with skins limited per licence, and platform/supplier licensing applies to every content and PAM vendor. Payments are overwhelmingly ACH/online banking, debit and wallets; credit-card funding is barred in several states. Responsible-gambling requirements (deposit/time limits, self-exclusion, 21+ KYC, geolocation) are state-mandated [individual state rules not re-verified this cycle].

The policy picture is the constraint. No state legalised iGaming in 2025 or 2026 sessions despite budget pressure (Maryland, New York and Illinois bills stalled); Maine is the only authorised-but-unlaunched market (AGA expected late 2026; rulemaking delays reported). Meanwhile the untaxed substitutes — sweepstakes casinos and skill machines — are drawing enforcement, which protects licensed iGaming in existing states but does not open new ones. For an operator, iGaming is the best-risk US vertical on margins and resilience, but entry is through partnership with a land-based licence holder in seven states, and the growth curve is now low-double-digit rather than 25%+.

segments.name: Traditional casino (retail slots & tables)
segments.headline: +0.9% to $4.44bn: stable but bifurcated — Nevada +3.1% on regional and baccarat strength while the Strip is flat and Vegas visitation falls; NJ and PA retail soft; RWNYC expansion lifting tables.
narrative: Land-based slot and table GGR was $4.44bn in August 2026 (+0.9% YoY, -0.9% MoM), with slots $3.25bn (+1.0%) and tables $885.9m (+2.1%). The AGA notes slot revenue was 'uneven across states' and credits table growth partly to Resorts World New York City's expansion to full-scale casino operations (the highest-grossing commercial property outside Nevada for three years running). Year-to-date traditional GGR is roughly $35.3bn, about +3% (derived), versus +2.3% to $50.94bn in CY2025 across 493 commercial casinos in 27 states; casino admissions in the five reporting states rose 5.3% in 2025.

Nevada, the largest single market, reported statewide win of $1,266.1m (+3.14%), the 66th consecutive month above $1bn, with Clark County $1,062.2m (+2.8%) but the Las Vegas Strip essentially flat at $684.1m (+0.70%) and downtown -3.0%. Growth came from the Boulder Strip (+17.4%), Washoe/Reno (+10.4%) and Laughlin, from statewide slots ($865.7m, +6.1%) and from Strip baccarat ($155m, +34.1% — more than all other Strip table games combined). The LVCVA counted 3.0m visitors (-4.3%), so Strip win is being held up by high-end table volatility and slot yield rather than footfall; MGM's Q3 Strip EBITDA fell 12% in parallel. Nevada's gaming tax (top marginal 6.75% of win) remains the lowest-cost regime in the country.

Elsewhere, Pennsylvania retail slots fell 1.3% to $213.9m (24,520 machines) and retail tables -18.1% to $66.4m, dragging total PA gaming revenue to $569.7m (-2.2%) with $249m of tax; New Jersey total gaming revenue fell 4.1% to $615.7m, with Atlantic City land-based outpacing iGaming for a second month only because iGaming slowed. Michigan's Detroit casinos reported July AGR of $112.6m (+5.3% on slots/tables). The five-state admissions data and the Nevada numbers point to a mature retail market growing low-single digits in nominal terms, with regional and new-build supply (Virginia, Nebraska, Illinois, New York downstate licences) the only sources of step-change.

For B2Tech, retail casino is relevant mainly as the licensing anchor: nearly every online skin in the US hangs off a land-based casino, racetrack or tribal licence. Land-based incumbents therefore control market access, which is why market-access fees and revenue shares are a structural cost of US online entry. The retail vertical itself — slots at ~73% of GGR — is a supplier and systems business (cabinets, CMS, cashless/payments) rather than an operator opportunity for a new entrant.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: State-by-state GGR taxation with a 2025–26 ratchet (NJ, IL, LA, MD), New York's 51% ceiling, a new federal 90% loss-deduction cap on players, and licences tethered to land-based assets.
narrative: The United States has no federal gambling regulator or federal online licence. Since Murphy v. NCAA (2018) struck down PASPA, each state (plus DC) legislates its own sports-betting regime; casino and iGaming authority likewise sits with state gaming commissions/control boards (e.g., NJ DGE/CCC, PGCB, NYSGC, NGCB, MGCB), while tribal gaming is governed federally under IGRA via compacts and the NIGC. The AGA counts 38 jurisdictions with commercial casinos and/or sports betting and 493 commercial casino locations in 27 states; seven states permit iGaming. Licences are typically anchored to a land-based casino, racetrack or tribal partner with a limited number of online 'skins', or to a capped number of standalone mobile licences (New York's model), and every platform, content, geolocation and payment supplier is separately licensed or registered. Fees, suitability investigations and renewal cycles are state-specific [not re-verified this cycle; see State of the States 2026 state chapters].

The tax base is gross gaming revenue (often 'adjusted' for promotional deductions, which several states have capped or phased out) rather than turnover, with two exceptions: the federal excise of 0.25% of sports handle (plus $50 per sportsbook employee) and Illinois' per-wager surcharge of $0.25 on the first 20m annual wagers and $0.50 thereafter, layered on a 20–40% graduated GGR rate. Online sports betting rates run from 6.75% (Nevada, Iowa) to 51% (New York, New Hampshire, Rhode Island); 2025 budget rounds lifted New Jersey to 19.75% for both online sports and iGaming (from 13%/15%), Louisiana to 21.5% online (from 15%), and Maryland to 20% online (from 15%); Ohio had already doubled to 20% in 2023 and resisted 40%. Casino GGR taxes range from Nevada's 6.75% top rate to effective rates above 50% in racino states; Pennsylvania's iGaming effective rate was ~45.6% in FY2025/26. The 2025 tax take was $17.86bn (+12.3%) per State of the States 2026 — the Feb-2026 tracker cited $18.09bn (+15.1%); the difference is unreconciled. August 2026 collections were $1.46bn (-1.5%), with sports betting tax -14.0%.

Player taxation changed on 1 January 2026: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed 4 Jul 2025) amended IRC §165(d) so that gambling losses are deductible only up to 90% of losses (still capped at winnings), creating taxable 'phantom' income for break-even bettors; the FAIR BET Act to restore 100% deductibility has been blocked in the House. Combined with Illinois' per-bet levy (passed through as customer surcharges by DraftKings and FanDuel), this raises the all-in cost of regulated betting precisely when an untaxed alternative (event contracts) is scaling — a point the AGA makes forcefully.

Direction of travel: fiscal pressure means 2027 state sessions (January–June) will again feature OSB/iGaming tax proposals; the regulator-level consensus (NCLGS, Louisiana GCB) is that hikes beyond ~20–25% push volume to grey channels. Expect more states to restrict promotional deductions and to add per-wager or 'integrity' levies rather than headline rate moves. iGaming legalisation remains the big unrealised revenue lever for states, but 2025–26 produced no new state. For an operator, model the US at a blended state tax of ~20–25% of GGR for OSB outside NY/IL, 15–50% for iGaming by state, plus market-access fees to land-based partners, 0.25% excise and licensing/compliance overhead in every state.

segments.name: Prediction markets, grey channels & enforcement
segments.headline: The defining regulatory fight: a 3rd/9th Circuit split on whether sports event contracts are CFTC-only 'swaps' or state-regulated gambling, cert petitions pending, a post-midterm Cruz bill, and $45bn of monthly untaxed volume.
narrative: The AGA's August release frames three untaxed channels as the reason state gaming tax collections 'could have been significantly higher': skill machines, sweepstakes casinos and 'prediction market' platforms offering sports contracts. Its cumulative estimate of state gaming tax foregone to event contracts since January 2025 has risen from roughly $0.5bn (Feb-2026 CY2025 tracker) to more than $1.56bn (Oct-2026), implying ~$1bn of claimed leakage in eight months — an advocacy figure, not a regulator statistic, but directionally consistent with sportsbook tax receipts falling 14% in August.

Volume data explain the alarm. Kalshi, a CFTC-registered designated contract market, reported $37.17bn of notional volume in August 2026 (down 7.3% from $40.1bn in July), with sports around 83% of July activity; Polymarket and its US venue added $8.16bn (-36.7% MoM). Combined volume of $45.33bn was the first monthly decline since August 2025, mirroring the regulated market's post-World-Cup drop, and remains roughly four times the $10.89bn regulated handle — although notional volume double-counts both sides and includes high-frequency and arbitrage flow, so it overstates consumer stake. Distribution through brokerages (Robinhood, Crypto.com) and the absence of state licensing, 21+ KYC parity, RG tooling or state tax are the competitive asymmetries.

The legal position is unresolved. On 6 April 2026 the Third Circuit (KalshiEX LLC v. Flaherty, 2–1) affirmed a preliminary injunction barring New Jersey from enforcing its gambling laws, holding Kalshi's sports contracts are likely 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act and that CFTC jurisdiction is exclusive (field and conflict pre-emption); the dissent called the products 'virtually indistinguishable' from sportsbook bets. On 28 August 2026 the Ninth Circuit ruled 3–0 the other way, refusing to enjoin the Nevada Gaming Control Board against Kalshi and Crypto.com on the basis that sports event contracts are not swaps. New Jersey, Robinhood and (reportedly) Crypto.com's exchange petitioned the Supreme Court between 2 and 11 September; no grant had been issued at the time of writing. The CFTC's own event-contract rulemaking (comments closed 30 April 2026) is pending, and tribes have joined states as plaintiffs.

Congress is now the second front. Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz intends to introduce, after the 3 November midterms, legislation preventing prediction markets from offering event contracts tied to gambling activity (including sports) unless authorised by the relevant state or tribal government — effectively re-fencing sports betting to the 38 legal jurisdictions and excluding Texas and other non-legal states. The AGA testified before the House Agriculture Committee (CFTC oversight) on 21 July 2026. The sweepstakes-casino front is further advanced: multiple states enacted prohibitions in 2025–26 and attorneys-general have escalated enforcement [state list not re-verified this cycle].

For an operator the implications cut both ways. If SCOTUS sides with the Ninth Circuit or the Cruz bill passes, regulated handle should recover meaningfully in 2027 and the value of state licences rises; if the Third Circuit view prevails, the US effectively gains a federally-licensed, untaxed national sports-betting channel and state OSB economics deteriorate further — in that world the rational play is to seek DCM/FCM exposure or B2B supply to prediction venues rather than more state skins. Either way, the binary is the single largest driver of 2027 US sportsbook value and should gate any B2C commitment.

segments.name: Market structure, payments & responsible gambling
segments.headline: A 38-jurisdiction patchwork anchored on land-based licences; payments via ACH/debit/wallets under UIGEA with state-level credit-card limits; RG and advertising rules set state-by-state — no national figures disclosed.
narrative: Structurally, the US commercial market comprises 38 jurisdictions with casinos and/or sports betting, 493 commercial casino locations in 27 states, seven iGaming states and a sports-betting footprint that grew by one state (Missouri, December 2025) in the year to mid-2026. Market access for online brands is almost universally tethered to land-based licence holders (casinos, racetracks, tribes) or to capped mobile licences, so incumbents extract market-access fees and revenue shares from entrants. The largest online markets by revenue in 2025 were New York, Illinois, New Jersey and Ohio for sports betting and Michigan, New Jersey and Pennsylvania for iGaming (~90% of the national total). New York's mobile sports market has eight live operators; the national top two (FanDuel, DraftKings) traded places on New York handle in July and August 2026, with Fanatics, BetMGM and Caesars a distant second tier — national share figures were not disclosed in this release [unverified].

Payments operate under the Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act (2006), which obliges banks and processors to block transactions for unlawful internet gambling and is the reason licensed operators run state-specific merchant codes and geolocation. Deposits are dominated by ACH/online banking, debit cards and digital wallets (PayPal/Venmo-type), with prepaid Play+ cards and cash-at-cage options; a number of states prohibit credit-card funding of online wagering accounts and several legislatures debated bans in 2025–26 [state detail not re-verified this cycle]. Mobile money is irrelevant in the US context; card-network coding and bank acceptance are the practical frictions, and processing costs are a material line in a 51%-tax state. No payments statistics are published in the AGA release (n/a).

Responsible-gambling and advertising rules are state-set and uneven: 21+ with identity verification is universal for online, geolocation is mandatory, and most states require deposit/time/loss-limit tooling, self-exclusion registers and problem-gambling funding earmarks; several (e.g., New York, Ohio, Massachusetts) have restricted 'risk-free'/'free bet' language and college-targeted marketing, and the industry's own AGA Responsible Marketing Code governs national advertising [specific state texts not re-verified this cycle]. Federal advertising legislation (SAFE Bet Act-type proposals) has not advanced. The prediction-market and sweepstakes channels operate outside these state RG regimes, which is both the AGA's consumer-protection argument and a competitive asymmetry for licensed operators.

The commercial read-through is that compliance, payments and marketing costs are duplicated across every state, and a national footprint requires 30+ separate licences, rule books and tax filings. This favours scaled incumbents and B2B suppliers (PAM, risk/trading, geolocation, payments, RG tooling) over new B2C entrants — and it is precisely the burden the federally-sheltered prediction markets avoid.

highlights.text: iGaming is the resilient vertical: +12.3% to $1.03bn in August (YTD $8.11bn, +17.4%) and now a larger monthly pool than sports betting, from only seven states; a partner-led iGaming entry (PAM/content/B2B) carries the best risk-adjusted economics in the US today.

The sports betting weakness is mostly margin, not demand: handle -0.7% vs revenue -15.6%, with 160bp of hold compression. A normal NFL/college hold in September–December mechanically restores revenue — a timing, not structural, component of the August print.

Event-driven upside is real and quantified: the World Cup lifted July handle +31.9% to $11.60bn and GGR +27.0% to $1.27bn, proving regulated operators can still capture marquee-event demand despite prediction-market competition.

Leadership at the top is contestable: DraftKings out-handled FanDuel in New York for two consecutive months ($614.0m vs $599.6m) while FanDuel kept the revenue lead ($64.0m vs $56.3m) — share is moving, which creates openings for differentiated product or pricing partners.

A pro-state legal/legislative resolution is now plausible: the Ninth Circuit's 3–0 ruling for Nevada, cert petitions pending, and a post-midterm Cruz bill requiring state/tribal authorisation would re-fence sports betting and recover a share of the ~$45bn/month of untaxed notional volume for licensed operators.
Enforcement against untaxed substitutes (sweepstakes casinos, skill machines) is intensifying, protecting licensed iGaming share in NJ/PA/MI and raising the value of holding a state licence.

Regional land-based pockets are growing (Boulder Strip +17.4%, Reno/Washoe +10.4%, Resorts World NYC expansion, Virginia/Nebraska new supply) — relevant for systems, cashless and content suppliers even as the Strip stalls.

lowlights.text: Regulated handle is structurally flat-to-down: the AGA confirms YoY declines in every non-World-Cup month since December 2025 while CFTC-registered prediction markets ran $37bn (Kalshi) of monthly notional volume with sports ~83% of activity — an untaxed, unlicensed national competitor that state regimes cannot currently reach in the Third Circuit.

Federal pre-emption risk: if SCOTUS adopts the Third Circuit's 'swaps' reading, sports event contracts gain a durable federal shield, state sportsbook taxes and licence values fall, and B2C OSB economics in 20%+ tax states deteriorate further.

Tax ratchet with no ceiling in sight: NJ to 19.75%, LA 21.5%, MD 20%, IL per-wager surcharge on top of 20–40%, NY at 51%; sportsbook tax receipts -14% in August will push more states to chase revenue in 2027 sessions precisely as margins compress.

Player-side federal tax hit from 2026 (90% loss-deduction cap) penalises high-volume and professional bettors — the customers most able to migrate to prediction markets or offshore — with the FAIR BET fix stalled.

iGaming expansion is stalled: no new state since Rhode Island (2024), Maine's launch has slipped, and 2025–26 legislative sessions failed in MD, NY and IL; growth is decelerating (+27.6% → +12.3%) and NJ slowed to +4.4% in August.

Land-based softness in gateway markets: Las Vegas visitation -4.3%, Strip win +0.7% only on volatile baccarat, PA retail tables -18.1%, NJ total gaming revenue -4.1% — the licence-anchor partners that entrants depend on face their own margin pressure and will price market access accordingly.

Data caveats: the headline comes from a trade body (AGA) compiling state reports, with Oklahoma missing for July–August and two AGA publications disagreeing on 2025 tax ($17.86bn vs $18.09bn); the $1.56bn 'lost tax' figure is an advocacy estimate, not a regulator statistic.

forecast.intro: The August print moves the 2026 trajectory from 'record year on autopilot' to 'low-to-mid single digit'. CY2025 commercial GGR was $78.72bn (+9.2%); January–August 2026 ran $53.84bn (+5.4%), but the mix has rotated: sports betting YTD growth has fallen to +4.0% and is likely to turn negative YoY for the full year as Q4 laps a 10.2%-hold 2025 and faces prediction-market leakage, while iGaming (+17.4% YTD) and traditional casino (~+3% YTD, derived) carry the total. The regulatory bridge is the Supreme Court cert decision and the Cruz bill: a pro-state outcome would re-fence handle in 2027; a pro-federal outcome would entrench an untaxed national competitor.
forecast.view: **Market:** we expect FY2026 commercial GGR of **$81.5–83.0bn (+3.5–5.5%)** [estimate], with sports betting GGR roughly **flat to -3%** for the year as hold normalises toward ~9.5% and handle stays negative ex-events, iGaming **+13–15%** (decelerating to high-single digits by mid-2027 absent new states), and traditional casino **+1–3%**. Online share rises to ~35–36% on mix. **Tax:** state gaming tax should still grow low-single digits in FY2026 on iGaming, but sportsbook tax will fall YoY, which we expect to trigger renewed OSB/iGaming tax proposals in at least a handful of 2027 sessions; expect promo-deduction caps and per-wager levies rather than 51%-style headline rates, and a possible Illinois per-wager repeal if volumes keep leaking. **Rules:** the base case is that the Supreme Court grants cert in the Kalshi cases with argument in 2027, keeping the status quo (state-by-state injunctions) through most of 2027; the Cruz bill has a credible path given bipartisan state/tribal support but faces a crowded lame-duck and a new Congress. **Leverage/operating economics:** at a 9–10% hold and 20–51% GGR tax, only the two scale leaders generate operating leverage in OSB; mid-tier operators will continue to exit or merge, and market-access fees will rise as land-based partners seek to offset flat retail. **Our stance for B2Tech:** do not commit B2C sportsbook capital ahead of the SCOTUS/Cruz binary; prioritise B2B supply into the seven iGaming states and position for either outcome of the event-contract fight (state-licensed OSB re-fencing, or DCM-adjacent supply).
watch: Supreme Court action on the New Jersey/Robinhood/Crypto.com cert petitions (conference calendar late 2026–early 2027) and any further district-court rulings in Maryland, Ohio, Arizona and tribal suits.
Introduction and co-sponsor count of the Cruz prediction-market bill after 3 Nov 2026; CFTC final rule on event contracts.
AGA September and October 2026 trackers (NFL/college full months): does handle return to YoY growth once the calendar effect reverses, and where does hold settle?
Kalshi/Polymarket monthly volumes and sports share — a sustained decline would indicate saturation; growth into the NFL season would confirm structural leakage.
2027 state budget sessions (Jan–Jun): OSB/iGaming tax proposals in NJ, OH, MI, MA, IL (HB 5143 per-wager repeal), and any iGaming legalisation in NY, MD, IL, IN.
Maine iGaming launch timing and rules; any eighth-state momentum.
FAIR BET Act progress to restore 100% gambling-loss deductibility; IRS guidance on event-contract tax treatment.
Las Vegas visitation and Strip win trend (LVCVA/NGCB) as a read on consumer discretionary spend and land-based partner health.
Sweepstakes-casino enforcement actions and new state prohibitions; AG settlements as a signal of state appetite to police grey channels.
